name: Terrible triad of the elbow
aliases: elbow dislocation with radial head and coronoid fractures

reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: The triad comprises a posterior or posterolateral elbow dislocation with fractures of the radial head and the coronoid process
It arises from a posterolateral rotatory mechanism, typically an axial load combined with valgus and external rotation
The elbow is highly unstable because both bony buttresses (radial head and coronoid) and the lateral collateral ligament are compromised

Management is usually surgical, fixing or replacing the radial head, addressing the coronoid and anterior capsule, and repairing the lateral collateral ligament, adding a medial repair or hinged fixator if instability persists
The radial head should be preserved or replaced rather than simply excised, in order to maintain stability
The goal is a concentrically reduced joint with a stable arc of motion permitting early mobilisation
CT is valuable to characterise the radial head and coronoid fractures and plan reconstruction
reference.pathophysiology: A fall generating axial loading with valgus and external rotation carries the elbow through posterolateral rotatory subluxation to frank dislocation. As the joint displaces, the radial head is driven against the capitellum and fractures, the coronoid process fractures as the trochlea rides over it, and the lateral collateral ligament complex avulses from the lateral epicondyle. The loss of these anterior, lateral and radiocolumnar stabilisers leaves the elbow grossly unstable and prone to redislocation, so restoration of each element is required to re-establish a stable, congruent joint.
additionalInvestigations: CT to characterise the radial head and coronoid fractures and plan fixation
Post-reduction radiographs to confirm concentric reduction
Examination and documentation of neurovascular status
Intra-operative assessment of the stable arc of motion
redFlags: Persistent instability or subluxation after reduction
Non-concentric reduction with a widened joint (drop sign)
reference.prognosis: Historically a difficult injury with poor results, but a systematic surgical protocol restoring the bony and ligamentous stabilisers has improved outcomes; stiffness, recurrent instability and post-traumatic arthritis remain recognised risks.
pitfalls: Treating the injury as a simple dislocation and mobilising an unstable joint
Excising the radial head rather than preserving or replacing it
Failing to confirm a concentric reduction on post-reduction imaging
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
